items.title: Oct. 21: Midwest inflation outpaces the nation, which was up 3.7% | Banking & Finance | fwbusiness.com
items.excerpt: Oct. 21: Midwest inflation outpaces the nation, which was up 3.7% | Banking & Finance | fwbusiness.com # Oct. 21: Midwest inflation outpaces the nation, which was up 3.7% * By Mike Marturello mmarturello@kpcmedia.com #### MIke Marturello * Author email (mmarturello@kpcmedia.com) * Oct 21, 2026 * 3 mins ago * 0 FORT WAYNE — Inflation in the Midwest has outpaced the nation, said data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Inflation, as measured by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ consumer price index, was up 4.2% in September for the Midwest while the national rate was 3.7%. Gasoline had a highest annual increase of 35.5% in the Midwest compared to 34.2% nationally year over year. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month. The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which has ticked higher since the war began in late February. “Inflation in the 3% range has proven to be a rather stubborn feature of the American economy in the past five years. And if employers aren’t providing adequate cost-of-living increases, workers are finding their paychecks just don’t stretch as far as they did a few years ago, leaving them with tough decisions on how to cover household expenses,” said Rachel Blakeman, director of the Community Research Institute at Purdue University Fort Wayne. “Things are going to be especially hard as we head into the holiday spending season as families and households balance costs vs. income and use of credit cards. With CPI well north of 3%, we can expect to see the Federal Reserve respond with higher interest rates as we close out 2026 and head into 2027.” The rise isn’t all linked to oil and gas, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices, The Associated Press reported. “With early voting now open in Indiana and many other states, we can expect to see voters taking their frustration about higher prices with them to the polls, just as they did in 2024,” said Blakeman. Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month and higher than economists had expected. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed’s 2% target. Higher inflation will likely put more pressure on the Fed to lift its key interest rate at its next meeting Oct. 27-28. Economists noted that the report showed price increases were spread more broadly across the economy than in recent months. “The report was worse than expected,” Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Bank, said in a note to clients. “Price increases were widespread ... affecting a range of durable goods, nondurables, and services.” Backing out the volatile energy and food sectors, Midwestern prices were up 3% in the Midwest and 2.6% nationally. Other notable year-over-year increases: • Household energy up 7.7% in the Midwest and 6.2% nationally with electricity up 8.8% regionally compared to 4.4% nationally. • Rent up 4.3% in the Midwest while nationally it was a 2.8%. • Food away from home (restaurants) was up 4.3% regionally and 3.5% in the United States. • Grocery increases were less in the Midwest with food at home up 1.5% compared to 1.8% nationally. Mike Marturello is the executive editor of KPC Media Group. **www.FWBusiness.com** 600 W. Main St. Fort Wayne, IN 46801 **Phone:** Phone: 260-426-2640 **Email:** llong@kpcmedia.com

items.title: Grocery Prices Sit 22% Above 2021 Levels as Near-Record Diesel Raises Costs From Farm to Store
items.excerpt: September price data show food at home costs 22.5% more than five years ago, while diesel above $6 a gallon adds pressure that has not fully reached store shelves. ... Americans are paying about 22% more for groceries than they did five years ago, and the latest federal price data arrived as diesel — the fuel that powers tractors, freight trucks and refrigerated trailers — holds near its record high. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' food-at-home index stood at 321.758 in September 2026, compared with 262.695 in September 2021, a 22.5% increase, according to BLS figures compiled by the St. Louis Fed. The monthly picture looks calmer. Grocery prices slipped 0.1% in September and were 1.8% higher than a year earlier, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in its latest Consumer Price Index release. But a slower annual rate does not erase five years of accumulated increases, and several of the foods most closely tied to a balanced diet are still rising faster than the grocery average. ... Fuel is what makes the next few months hard to call. The national average price of diesel was $6.33 a gallon on Oct. 16, up 68% from $3.76 before the U.S.-Iran war began, according to AAA figures cited by the Associated Press. Diesel hit a record $6.53 in September. No federal agency has yet measured how much of that cost will reach retail food prices, and economists quoted by the AP said much of it has not shown up so far. ... The September report shows a split grocery aisle. Fresh fruits were up 4.9% from a year earlier, fruits and vegetables overall rose 3.7%, coffee climbed 7.1%, and beef rose 3.5%, according to the BLS detailed tables. Eggs fell 20.6%, and dairy dipped 0.7%, which helped hold the overall grocery figure down. ... Eating out remains the bigger budget strain. Prices for food away from home rose 3.5% over the year, nearly double the grocery rate. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service now forecasts grocery prices will rise 2.4% in 2026, with fresh vegetables up 5.7% and beef and veal up 9.4%, while eggs are expected to fall 29.4%. The AP reported that USDA's forecast before the war called for a 1.7% grocery increase this year.

items.title: US inflation rose slightly last month after 2 years of steady cooling but remained low
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — Inflation in the United States ticked up in October, driven by costlier rents, used cars and air fares, a sign that price increases might be leveling off after having slowed in September to their lowest pace since 2021. Consumer prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 2.4% in September. It was the first rise in annual inflation in seven months. From September to October, prices edged up 0.2%, the same as the previous month. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, “core” prices rose 3.3% from a year earlier, the same as in September. From September to October, core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Over the long run, core inflation at that pace would exceed the Fed’s 2% target. ... An uptick in prices, if sustained, could stir concerns in financial markets that progress in taming inflation may be slowing. It might also make the Federal Reserve less inclined to cut its key interest rate in the coming months, as its officials have previously indicated they likely would.
